chat.author: Alexey Melnikov
chat.text: No strong opinion, but I prefer fewer options

chat.author: Alexey Melnikov
chat.text: So compress then sign is my preference

chat.author: Russ Housley
chat.text: No, a Base64-encoded digital signature will not compress well.   Here is why...

chat.author: Russ Housley
chat.text: Digital signatures are the output of cryptographic algorithms (like RSA, ECDSA, or Ed25519). By design, these outputs are highly random.

chat.author: Russ Housley
chat.text: Base64encoding takes 3 bytes of binary data and represents them using 4 ASCII characters.

chat.author: Russ Housley
chat.text: Base64 instantly increases size by roughly 33%.

chat.author: Russ Housley
chat.text: However, entropy remains high. Even though the signature is now restricted to a set of 64 characters, the sequence of those characters remains random.

chat.author: Russ Housley
chat.text: An attempt to compress a Base64 signature, the compression algorithm might shrink slightly, but it will almost never get the data back down to its original raw binary size.

chat.author: Alexey Melnikov
chat.text: I think Russ is just arguing that there is no point compressing after signing
